s: Æsculapius is a deity of healing, worshipped from the beginning and especially associated with Epidaurus. According to the Epidaurian tradition, he was born there to Apollo and Coronis, though Arsinoe is also named as his mother and other accounts differ. Exposed on Mount Myrgion, he was fed by a she-goat and guarded by a watch-dog; he became renowned for healing sickness and raising the dead. His worship spread from Epidaurus to Athens, Pergamum, Smyrna, Cyrene, Crete, and many other places. Temples, shrines, altars, and statues mark this spread, including sites at Sicyon, Titane, Argos, Booneta, and Epidaurus Limera. Dragons, particularly tawny tame ones, were sacred to him: at Sicyon he was said to have come from Epidaurus as a dragon, while at Epidaurus Limera altars stood where a sacred dragon disappeared. His images varied, including a beardless gold-and-ivory image, a veiled statue, and a seated white-stone statue beside Hygiea.

Hippolytus, son of Theseus, was sent to Pittheus at Trœzen to be raised and rule. Phædra’s unsuccessful love and Theseus’s curses were attributed to his death. At Trœzen he has a precinct, temple, statue, priest, yearly sacrifices, race-course, house, and tomb near the temple of Themis; maidens offer hair before marriage. The people honor him in heaven as the Charioteer.

Pittheus is associated with a three-seat monument at Troezen where he and two others were said to judge. He built the oldest-known temple of Thearian Apollo, taught language, erected an altar to the Muses, and united Hyperea and Anthea into Troezen.

The Acropolis is a precipitous, walled place with one approach. Its marble-roofed entrance contains vestibules, the shrine of Wingless Victory, paintings, Hermes called Propylæus, and Graces attributed to Socrates. Within are statues, paintings, monuments of mythic and historical battles, the temples of Athene Polias and Pandrosus, sacred offerings, Callimachus’s golden lamp, and Athene’s olive. Its notable votives include brazen images and a chariot; its walls were largely attributed to Pelasgians, except Cimon’s part.
Odysseus takes the Palladium from Ilium, appears before Nausicaa and her maids, wins Penelope's suitors' race, and sleeps with Circe in her cave.
Palladium is a statue of Athene carried from Ilium to Italy by Æneas; the Argives claimed its removal caused Ilium’s fall.

Orestes, son of Agamemnon, was accused of shedding his mother’s blood, housed and fed in a tent at Troezen until gradually purified, with Hippocrene water linked to his purgations. Tried at the Areopagus, he escaped punishment and erected an altar of Athene. After Cylarabes died childless, he gained Argos, Arcadian territory, and Sparta. Spartan tradition credits him with bringing the Orthian Artemis cult; his tomb was at Sparta.

has brazen bust [in the temple of Hera among the Samians] When Alcibiades had a strong Athenian fleet near Ionia, most of the Ionians courted him, and the Samians displayed a brazen bust of him in the temple of Hera. Their support changed after the Athenian defeat at Aegospotami.

Cypselus, a Corinthian tyrant descended through ancestors from Melas, was hidden in a chest by his mother at birth to evade the Bacchidae. He later possessed the chest; his descendants, the Cypselidae, dedicated it at Olympia.

Hygiea is a deity worshipped by those seeking propitiation. Her statues include one seated near Æsculapius at Argos and a hard-to-see image at Æsculapius’s temple at Titane, concealed by women’s shorn hair and a Babylonish garment.

rules Elis [after winning the footrace at Olympia] Epeus won the footrace held by Endymion at Olympia and became king, after which his people were first called Epeans. He married Anaxiroe and had a daughter, Hyrmina, but no male heir.

is_named_for Ares [because Ares was first tried there] The Areopagus was so called because Ares was first tried there, and Orestes was also said to have been tried there for killing his mother. Those acquitted before it offered sacrifices at the nearby temple of the Venerable Ones, and two white stones used by defendants and plaintiffs were called Rigour-of-the-law and Impudence. Ephialtes was remembered as having tried to discredit the legislation of the Areopagus.

l: the contest between Poseidon and Athene for the soil of Attica, Description of Greece
s: The contest between Poseidon and Athene for the soil of Attica is depicted behind the Parthenon, with Athene showing the olive tree and Poseidon showing water.

l: the statue of Athene, Description of Greece
s: The statue of Athene is a full-length ivory-and-gold object. It wears a foot-length tunic and Medusa’s ivory-worked head on its breast, holds a four-cubit Victory and a spear, has a shield and possible dragon Erichthonius, and stands on a base depicting Pandora’s birth.

l: Pericles son of Xanthippus, Description of Greece
s: Pericles son of Xanthippus, an Athenian statesman, was commemorated by an Acropolis statue and an Academy-road tomb; later comparison said Lycurgus added more treasury wealth than he collected.

Olympiodorus is an Athenian general celebrated for restoring Athenian hopes. Elected amid remembered ancestral fame, he defeated Macedonians, captured the Museum, recovered Piraeus and Munychia, won at Eleusis, gained Aetolian aid against Cassander, and helped Phocians at Elatea. Athens, Eleusis, and the Phocians honored him with memorials.
Darius, illegitimate son of Artaxerxes, deposed Sogdius with Persian commonalty support, usurped Artaxerxes’s kingdom, became king, and summoned Polydamas to Susa after hearing of his exploits.

besiege Œniadæ [after gathering forces from their towns] The Acarnanians were defeated by the Messenians at Œniadæ, then gathered forces from their towns and besieged the Messenians there. They maintained the blockade until the Messenians escaped, losing many men in the fighting.

Epidaurus is a city in Argolis, associated with differing traditions about its ancestry and with the exposure of the infant Æsculapius, whose worship originated there. Pityreus yielded its land to Deiphontes and the Argives, after which Epidauria became especially sacred to Æsculapius. Epidaurus contains his open-air temple and dedications to Epione, Dionysus, Artemis, Aphrodite, Hera, and Cissæan Athene, as well as Melissa’s tomb.

Sicyon is a place near Corinth, connected by road to Phlius and serving as the starting point for roads to Phlius and Titane. Its people preserve traditions of Ægialeus founding Ægialea and of a burnt temple of Apollo on the citadel. Nearby temples and groves honor Hera, Demeter, Proserpine, and the Eumenides.

Elis is a Peloponnesian people and country, originally settled from Calydon and other parts of Ætolia; its inhabitants were successively called Epeans and Eleans. Formerly considered especially orderly, it is fertile in fruits and notably in flax, including flax said to grow nowhere else in Greece. It contains Samicum, has Cyllene as a harbor, and includes a city with civic, athletic, and religious sites. Its people are associated with a longstanding dislike of horses and with a supposed curse affecting mares bred with he-asses. What matters most is Elis's control of Olympia and the Olympian games. It preserves Olympian rites, sacrifices, altars, temples, offerings, victor records, and statues; controls admission and rules for contests; imposes athletic fines; proclaims victors; and changes the programme of events. It repeatedly contests Pisa's attempts to conduct the games, refuses to recognize the 104th Olympiad conducted by Pisæans and Arcadians, and organizes umpires according to its tribes. Its religious life includes worship of Sosipolis and Ilithyia and sacrifices to Zeus, Pelops, Hercules, and others. Its history begins with settlement, conflicts involving Hercules, disputes with Pisa and Arcadians over Olympia, the settlement of Oxylus, and Iphitus's revival of the games. Elis participates in the Trojan war and the Persian invasion, supplies the Messenian colony at Cyllene, and reluctantly allies with the Lacedæmonians in Attica. It later fights the Lacedæmonians alongside Mantineans and Athenians. After losing territory to Arcadians, its tribes fall from twelve to eight. It joins Macedonians under Philip, attacks the Lacedæmonians, then fights Macedonians after Alexander's death. Corruption connected with Philip brings faction, followed by a Messenian intervention. Aristotimus briefly rules with Antigonus's support before being deposed and killed. Finally, after hardship and Lacedæmonian invasions, Elis yields Lepreum and other subject communities, destroys its fortifications, and admits the Lacedæmonians to Olympia.
Phlius, chief town of Phliasia near Titane and Sicyon, was taken by Rhegnidas after the Heraclidæ returned; its citadel, sanctuaries, monuments, and public buildings preserve its traditions.
The Museum, a hill within Athens’ old walls opposite the Acropolis and associated with Musaeus, was fortified by Demetrius and served Macedonians as a refuge until Olympiodorus captured it.

Erechtheum is a place containing altars to Supreme Zeus, Poseidon, Erechtheus, Butes, and Hephaestus, paintings of Butes’ family, and a sea-water well that roars in the south wind beside Poseidon’s trident mark.

Gythium is a seaside town of the Eleutherolacones, one of their 18 cities, about 30 stades from Ægiæ, with Las on its right. Local tradition says Apollo and Hercules jointly built it after contesting the tripod. Its market-place has their statues, and it has sanctuaries of Dionysus, Carnean Apollo, Ammon, Æsculapius, Demeter, Poseidon, and Athene; nearby maritime Laconia supplies purple-dye shellfish.

Bœæ, founded by Bœus, stands at the head of the Bay of Bœæ opposite Cythera, including a mainland promontory near Platanistus. It worships Artemis Saviour, contains a temple of Apollo and Nymphæum, and has a road to the temple of Artemis Limnas.

Nemea, 15 stades from Cleonæ, contains Nemean Zeus’s temple with fallen roof and missing statue, Opheltes’s walled tomb with altars, and Adrastea; Argives sacrifice to Zeus and hold winter armored running contests.

l: battle of Marathon, Description of Greece
s: The Battle of Marathon was fought at Marathon, where the Athenians defeated the Persians, who lost ships while retreating. Its Persian spoil was used for Phidias's brazen statue of Athene. The Athenians buried their dead, the Platæans, and slaves there, honoured them as heroes, and reported Echetlæus fighting.

l: battle of Chaeronea, Description of Greece
s: is_a beginning of sorrows for the Greeks The battle of Chaeronea is described as the beginning of sorrows for the Greeks. Its aftermath brought enslavement and Macedonian domination to both Greeks who had not attended the battle and those who had fought against the Macedonians.

After Alexander’s death, the Athenians and several allied Greek cities took up arms against Macedonian control. Leosthenes led the coalition and initially achieved notable successes, but his death caused widespread discouragement and contributed to the failure of the effort.

l: Macedonian occupation of Athens, Description of Greece
s: Macedonian forces first occupied Munychia and later the Piraeus and the long walls. After Cassander became king, he captured Panactus and Salamis and supported rulers over Athens, while Demetrius son of Antigonus later maintained a garrison and fortified the Museum.

l: Olympiodorus's liberation of Athens, Description of Greece
s: ended Macedonian occupation of Athens [by taking the Museum and freeing the city] Olympiodorus led old men and young men against the Macedonians and defeated them in battle. He captured the Museum, thereby freeing Athens from the Macedonians, and later recovered the Piraeus and Munychia and defeated Macedonian forces at Eleusis.

is_king_of Megara Theagenes of Thasos outboxed Euthymus while attempting to win both the boxing and pancratium prizes in the same Olympiad. Because he was exhausted in the boxing contest, he did not receive the pancratium crown and was fined two talents, one for offending the god and one for injuring Euthymus; he paid the divine fine in the 76th Olympiad and thereafter did not compete again as a boxer.

Olympia is a place beyond Scillus across the Alpheus, immediately associated with the river, the Olympic games, sacred rites, athletic training, and a dense collection of temples, groves, monuments, and offerings. Its central sacred area is the Altis, the grove of Zeus, containing the Temple of Zeus, the temple of Hera, the grove of Pelops, a great altar, many lesser altars, treasuries, statues, paintings, and votive gifts. Outside Altis stood the workshop of Phidias; oil protected the ivory of the Zeus statue from dampness. A wild olive behind Hera’s temple supplied the crowns awarded to victors. Its traditions begin with contests for power and divine competition: Endymion’s sons competed there for a kingdom, Pelops established control, and early races were connected with the Idæan Dactyli and Zeus, Cronos, Apollo, Hermes, and Ares. Clymenus established games and an altar to Hercules and the Curetes; Iphitus later renewed the contests, which expanded from running to wrestling, boxing, horse-races, the pentathlum, and the pancratium. The restoration and control of the contests caused disputes among Elis, Pisa, and the Arcadians. Exclusion from Olympia’s contests and privileges led the Lacedæmonians to fight Elis; after submitting, Elis permitted them to sacrifice and compete. The quoit of Iphitus records an armistice between Elis and the Olympians. Olympia’s games were supported by training grounds for races, the pentathlum, and wrestling, as well as horse-racing facilities. Its rules had force: Mount Typæum was the threatened punishment site for women entering forbidden contests, and statues warned against cheating and bribery. Victories were proclaimed and preserved through statues, inscriptions, chariots, horses, and monuments, though not every victor was represented. These commemorated athletes such as Euthymus, Diagoras and his family, Theagenes, and others, alongside horse-breeders, rulers, seers, and military figures. The place also accumulated dedications from individuals, cities, and foreign communities: treasuries, bronze monuments, trophies, and offerings from many named peoples and places. Thus Olympia unfolds from sacred and contest traditions into an enduring venue where worship, competition, political conflict, commemoration, and public offerings continually gather.

l: brazen statue of Athene, Description of Greece
s: The brazen statue of Athene, made by Phidias from Persian spoil taken at Marathon, bore Mys's shield carvings of Lapiths battling Centaurs, outlined by Parrhasius; sailors approaching Athens could see its spearpoint and helmet plume from Sunium.

Pan, a deity, meets Philippides near the Parthenian forest, promises aid to Athene at Marathon, and is honoured by the Athenians; it has a cave near Marathon and is worshipped with Dionysus at Erasinus.

The Academy, once owned privately, became a gymnasium. Its surroundings held precincts, altars, and Plato’s tomb; Prometheus’ altar began torch races, while the road contained tombs of Athenian soldiers and notable men.

l: Thrasybulus son of Lycus, Description of Greece
s: Thrasybulus son of Lycus had the first tomb on the road to the Academy. He was described as one of the most famous Athenians and was praised for marching from Thebes with only sixty men, overthrowing the Thirty Tyrants, and persuading the divided Athenians to reconcile.

The Æginetans inhabit Ægina, speak Doric language and manners after Argive settlers mixed with earlier inhabitants, and become a naval power greater than the Athenians. They provide the second-largest fleet in the Persian War, are expelled by Athenians to Lacedæmonian-given Thyrea, then recover Ægina after Athenian triremes are captured.

revolt_from Lacedæmonians [the Helots who were Messenians] The Messenians captured at Eira were forcibly incorporated among the Helots. In the 79th Olympiad, the Messenian Helots revolted again from the Lacedæmonians and went to Mount Ithome.

Ithome is a mountain encircling Messene, with a small town enlarged by Messenians who abandoned inland towns after losses, desertions, and pestilence. Its high, difficult access made it their stronghold and a defensive position behind their army. A sacred enclosure of Zeus stood on its summit; its neglected worship was restored by Glaucus. After a siege of about five months at the end of the twenty-year first Messenian War, the Messenians evacuated Ithome and the Lacedæmonians razed it. Later it was a stronghold of revolting Messenian Helots, held recovered Mysteries, and contained Messene's citadel, Clepsydra, and Zeus's annual feast.

are_renamed_from Epeans [under Eleus] The Eleans were formerly called Epeans and took their later name during the reign of Eleus. They fought Hercules with assistance from Pylos and Pisa, and later participated in conflicts involving the Dorians, Persians, Lacedæmonians, Macedonians, and other Greeks.

is_foretold_to_be excellent in Philosophy [by divine prophecy] Plato's tomb was near the Academy. The text says that the Deity foretold Plato would become most excellent in Philosophy, and that Socrates received this indication in a dream of a swan flying into his bosom on the night before Plato was to become his pupil.

Adrastus fled Argos, went to Polybus at Sicyon, and gained chief power there after Polybus died. He later returned to Argos and became its king. He built a temple beside Hera’s, with altars to Pan and the Sun God. Honored at Megara, he died there of old age and sorrow for Ægialeus.

Oropus is a place near the sea between Attica and Tanagra, originally in Bœotia and later Athenian after Thebes’ capture; it contains Amphiaraus’ temple, worship, oracle, and healing fountain for coin offerings.

Nemesis is honoured in a seaside temple at Rhamnus, especially implacable toward haughty men; Phidias fashioned her marble statue from Persian-brought stone, with crown, stags, Victories, apple branch, and bowl.

Helen is a figure linked to competing local traditions. She is mother of Iphigenia and is associated with Sparta, Therapne, Rhodes, and Leuce. The Lacedæmonians say she was buried with Menelaus at Therapne; the Rhodians say that, after Menelaus died, Nicostratus and Megapenthes drove her away and Polyxo had her hanged, leading to worship of Helen Hung on the Tree. On Leuce she married Achilles, though another account disputes Achilles as her suitor.

is_a river Cephisus is a river crossed along the route. Near it are statues of Mnesimaches and his son, who is shown cutting off his hair as a votive offering to the river, and on the other side is an ancient altar to Milichian Zeus.

Perseus, Danaë’s son, is a figure credited with killing and beheading Medusa, whose head he displayed to the Greeks. He was said to have warred with Dionysus before becoming friendly with him. At Larissa, while showing skill with quoits, he unintentionally killed his grandfather Acrisius; ashamed, he exchanged kingdoms with Megapenthes and founded Mycenæ. He received greatest honours at Seriphus and honours at a hero-chapel near Mycenæ.
is_a hero Lacius is identified as a hero who gives his name to a township.

l: grove of Lacius, Description of Greece
s: gives_name_to township named for Lacius The grove of Lacius lies a little farther along the road and is associated with the hero Lacius. A tomb of Nicocles of Tarentum, an altar to Zephyrus, and a temple of Demeter and Proserpine are located there.

Phytalus received Demeter into his house, and she gave him the fig tree. His tomb bears an inscription commemorating this event and the lasting fame of his race; Theseus was later purified after slaying Phytalus's progeny.

l: temple of Cyamites, Description of Greece
s: is_named_for Cyamites [called the temple of Cyamites] The temple of Cyamites is a small temple beside the road. The account does not establish whether Cyamites was the first person to sow beans or a hero whose name became associated with the temple.

The Eleusinian Mysteries are privately managed by Eleusinians as rites of Demeter and Proserpine, performed by Celeus’s daughters; after Eleusis’s battle with Athens, their contents remained forbidden to uninitiated people.

The Rheti are river-like seawater channels, possibly flowing underground from the Euripus near Chalcis; sacred to Proserpine and Demeter, priest-only fishing waters, they once marked the Eleusinian-Athenian boundary.

have_private_management_of Eleusinian Mysteries [under the peace settlement] The Eleusinians fought the Athenians, and peace left them Athenian in other respects while allowing them private management of the Mysteries. Their women were said to have first danced and sung to Demeter at the Well of Callichorus, and their territory contained temples, tombs, and other sacred sites.

Æacus is remembered as Ægina’s only early king: he built civic and sacred works, aided Greek envoys during drought by appealing to Pan-Hellenian Zeus, sought settlers and defenses for the island, and later judged Telamon over Phocus’s death.

l: Artemis the Saviour, Description of Greece
s: Artemis the Saviour has a temple and statues in the market-place of Troezen. Theseus was said to have built the temple and given her this title after returning from Crete.

Alcathous, son of Pelops and son-in-law of Megareus, killed the Cithæron lion, gained Megareus’s daughter and succeeded to Megara’s kingdom. As king he built temples, began Megara’s citadel and wall after sacrifice to the Prodromi, and rebuilt the wall after its destruction, with Apollo’s aid. His family suffered: Periboea went to Crete, Ischepolis died hunting, and Alcathous killed Callipolis in error.

l: battle between Eleusis and Athens, Description of Greece
s: Battle between Eleusis and Athens kills Erechtheus and Immaradus; peace makes Eleusinians Athenians while preserving their private management of the Mysteries.

Hecate, a deity, is honored by Æginetans above other gods through annual rites attributed to Orpheus; her depictions include Scopas's stone statue at Argos and Myron's one-headed, one-bodied wooden statue.

Ægialeus is an Autochthon said by the people of Sicyon to have first dwelt in their region. Ægialus was named after him; he founded Ægialea, whose citadel site later held Apollo’s temple, and fathered Europs.
Lysippus is a sculptor who made Muses in a neighbouring temple and statues at Olympia, including Troilus and Xenarches; his work also helps Pausanias date Chilon’s possible war.
The Isthmus extends from the sea near Cenchreae to the sea near Lechaeum, making Peloponnese a peninsula; canal-cutting attempts failed, leaving visible excavation remains.

The Isthmian games were Greek athletic games held at the Isthmus and established by Sisyphus in honour of Melicerta, also called Palæmon, after his burial. They endured Corinth’s destruction by Mummius, moved to Sicyon while Corinth was desolate, and returned when Corinth was rebuilt. They occasioned a truce, were avoided by Elis according to disputed traditions, and featured recorded victories by Nicasylus, Epitherses, and Lycus.

The Heraclidæ were a group whose return to the Peloponnese, during Tisamenus’s reign, was led by Temenus, Cresphontes, and the sons of Aristodemus. Claiming Argos through these leaders, they returned to Messenia two generations after Nestor’s death. Their return with the Dorians disturbed nearly all the Peloponnese, expelled rulers from Lacedæmon, Argos, and Messenia, and brought Dorian settlers and population changes.

Corinth is a city containing the Isthmus of Corinth and notable structures including the Theatre, white-stone Stadium, Temple of Poseidon, Well of Glauce, and Odeum. Its name is attributed either to Corinthus or, in Eumelus’s account, to Ephyre, Marathon, and the Ephyræans. Ancient Corinthians no longer inhabit it. It was held by a Macedonian garrison under Antigonus until Aratus attacked, defeated the garrison, and helped free it. After Corinth joined the Achaean revolt, Romans destroyed it; it was later rebuilt by Julius Caesar, inhabited by Roman colonists, and given an imperial government. It lies on the coastal road toward Sicyon, amid sites marked by wars and fires, and is associated with Isthmian games and truce traditions.

Epopeus, king of Ægialea from Thessaly, gained the kingdom when Corax died childless. He defeated the Thebans over Antiope despite a wound, sacrificed to Athene, built temples to Athene, Artemis, and Apollo, and died from his neglected wound. His great shrine of Athene was struck by lightning, leaving its altar before his tomb.
A king of disputed parentage, Sicyon became associated with the region and city thereafter called Sicyonia and Sicyon, giving them his name.

is_named_after Sicyon [when Sicyon became king] Sicyonia received its name after Sicyon became king, replacing the earlier name Ægialea. It later became part of Argolis after the Sicyonians became Dorians.

is_joined_by Corinth The Achaean confederacy included Corinth, which joined its war against the Romans. Critolaus, appointed commander in chief, persuaded the Achaeans and many Greeks outside the Peloponnese to revolt.
Cenchreae, one of Corinth's seaports, was said to be named after Cenchrias or Cenchreus and contained sanctuaries, temples, and a brazen Poseidon statue.
Lechaeum, Corinth's seaport named after Leches, contains a temple and brazen statue of Poseidon.

l: Theatre of Corinth, Description of Greece
s: The Theatre was one of the great sights of Corinth. Near it stood the temple of Athene the Bridler, a wooden statue of Hercules attributed to Daedalus, a temple of Jupiter Capitolinus, and an old gymnasium.
Bellerophon, honoured with a temple at Corinth, is aided by Athene, who breaks and bridles Pegasus and gives him the horse.

Neleus, son of Cretheus, fled Pelias at Iolcus, received Aphareus’ maritime Messenian lands including Pylos, and established his government there. With the Pelasgians of Iolcus he expelled Pylos, brought Pylos renown, and possessed oxen descended from Iphiclus’ herd.

Nestor, son of Neleus, is associated with Pylos, where traditions place his house, image, oxen’s stall, and tomb. Some said he was raised in Gerenia or fled there after Hercules took Pylos. He recovered Machaon’s bones and, after Aphareus’s sons died, received and ruled Messenia; his descendants were later expelled by the Dorians and returning Heraclidæ.
Lerna is a seaside place about forty stades from Argos, bordered by the Pontinus and Amymone, with sacred places and rites for several deities and associations with descents to Hades.

Medea becomes Corinth’s queen after being summoned from Iolcus, makes Jason king, and provides incantations to tame violent winds. Accounts dispute her children’s fate; one says she hides them in Hera’s temple, leaves Corinth, and gives Sisyphus the kingdom.
Phocus, son of Thetis and father of Panopeus and Crisus, was killed by Telamon and Peleus when Peleus threw a quoit during a pentathlon; they fled Ægina, and his tomb stood near the Hall of Æacus.

The Dorians are a people who came from Mount Œta and, during the return of the Heraclidæ, sought entry into the Peloponnese under the sons of Aristomachus, with Oxylus as leader. They displaced Achæans, drove out descendants of Neleus, and occupied territory. They assigned Argos to Temenus; Cresphontes obtained Messenia, where older Messenians accepted him and land was divided among Dorians. They colonized Hermione and seized Sicyon under Phalces, after which Sicyonians became Dorians and joined Argolis. They entered Phlius amid divided response, destroyed Amyclæ, besieged Helus, made its inhabitants Helots, expelled Achæans from Geronthræ, and settled colonists there.

Acrocorinth is the summit of a hill above Corinth. Briareus awarded it to the Sun after litigation with Poseidon, and the Sun gave it to Aphrodite. It contains temples to many gods, including Aphrodite, and a fountain associated with Asopus or Pirene.

l: destruction of Corinth by Mummius, Description of Greece
s: is_carried_out_by Mummius [as general of the Roman army] Mummius, the Roman army's general, destroyed Corinth after the Corinthians participated in the Achaean war against Rome. While the city lay desolate, the Isthmian games were held at Sicyon.

l: rebuilding of Corinth by Julius Caesar, Description of Greece
s: is_carried_out_by Julius Caesar Julius Caesar was said to have rebuilt Corinth and instituted the Imperial form of government at Rome. After the rebuilding, the Isthmian games returned to Corinth, and the city was inhabited by Roman colonists.

A burnt-down temple near Corinth, on the coastal road toward Sicyon. Its identity and destruction are disputed: one account calls it Apollo’s temple, destroyed by Pyrrhus, son of Achilles; another says Corinthians dedicated it to Olympian Zeus and that accidental fire destroyed it.

Olympian Zeus is a deity worshipped at Olympia. Games honor him, and Elis built his temple and statue from spoils after destroying Pisa. His gold-and-ivory statue holds Victory and a jeweled eagle-bearing sceptre. Worship unfolds through sacrifices, votive offerings, and several altars, especially Olympia’s greatest altar made from sacrificial debris.

l: genealogy of Sicyon’s kings, Description of Greece
s: The reported succession begins with Ægialeus, followed by his son Europs, Europs’s son Telchis, and Telchis’s son Apis. Apis’s son was Thelxion, followed by Ægyrus, Thurimachus, and Leucippus. Leucippus had only one daughter, Chalcinia, who bore Peratus to Poseidon; Peratus was raised by Leucippus and succeeded him as king. Peratus’s son was Plemnæus, whose son Orthopolis was reared by Demeter; Orthopolis’s daughter was Chrysorthe, whose son was Coronus, father of Corax and Lamedon.

Polydorus, son and successor of Alcamenes, was king of Sparta during the first war with the Messenians; valued for moderation and mercy, he was murdered by Polemarchus and afterward honored by the Lacedæmonians.
Sicyon, first built in the plain by Ægialeus, was later razed by Demetrius, who built the present city on the citadel, with temples, tombs, theaters, a market-place, gymnasium, and sanctuaries.

Pelops is a Lydian from Asia Minor who came to Pisæa and Olympia, deposed Œnomaus, occupied them, and took neighboring territory from Epeus. Before racing Oenomaus, Elis tradition says he sacrificed to Athene Cydonia; after defeating him, he buried Hippodamia’s suitors in a common tomb and gave them annual funeral rites. Elis also credited him with the first temple to Hermes in the Peloponnese and sacrifice to Hermes for Myrtilus’s murder. He made the contest to Olympian Zeus more famous, and his race with Œnomaus was represented at Olympia. Honoured there nearly as highly among heroes as Zeus among gods, he received an annual black-ram sacrifice; his remains and a lost shoulder-blade tradition were associated with Pisa, Elis, Troy, and Euboea.
Phlias, son of Dionysus and Aræthyrea, is said to give his name to the land, sail in Argo, marry Chthonophyle, and have Andromedas.

Temenus, son of Aristomachus, occupied and fortified Temenium against Tisamenus and the Achæans. He made Deiphontes his general and associate, gave him his beloved daughter Hyrnetho, and seemed likely to name them heirs. His sons killed him over that suspicion.

includes Sicyonia [after the Sicyonians became Dorians] Argolis included Sicyon after the Sicyonians became Dorians. The coast of Argolis also included Epidaurus and Trœzen, which later joined the Achæan league.

Achaia, the Peloponnese’s second division, was formerly Ægialus, inhabited by Ionians until Achæans displaced them. After Heraclidæ expelled Tisamenus and his sons from Lacedæmon and Argos, they arrived with an army; it borders Elis at Larisus, once said to be Araxus.

is_a chief town of the Arcadians Megalopolis, the chief town of the Arcadians, was captured by Cleomenes during a truce. About one third of its inhabitants were captured or slain, while Philopœmen and more than two thirds of the people escaped and were received by the Messenians.
Sellasia, site of battle, saw Antigonus and the Achæans defeat Cleomenes, after which it was enslaved and Lacedæmon captured.

Aratus, son of Clinias, overthrows Nicocles at Sicyon, restores isonomy and refugees’ property, and brings Sicyon into the Achæan league. He campaigns against enemies and helps free Corinth, wins Olympia’s chariot-race, receives Corinthian honors, is poisoned by Philip, and is buried in Sicyon’s Arateum.

The Achæan league, led by Aratus after he forced Sicyon into it, was openly hostile to the Lacedæmonians. It fought Cleomenes, defeated him at Sellasia with Antigonus, expanded through several joining cities, and had the Messenians join, leave after conflict, then rejoin after those responsible for Philopœmen’s death were punished.

Agis, son of Archidamus and Spartan king, succeeded Archidamus, led the Lacedæmonians against Elis despite an earthquake withdrawal, ravaged Elis, attacked Attica, and fortified Decelea. Before dying fighting Macedonians, he affirmed Leotychides as his son, but Agesilaus excluded him from kingship.

is_created_by Polycletus [in white stone] The Argives erected a statue to Milichian Zeus after the people killed Bryas and the thousand picked men who supported him. The statue was made by Polyclitus in white stone.

Lycian Apollo, also called Apollo the Wolf-God, was honored in Argos after Danaus read a wolf’s victory over a bull as a sign of his own victory over Gelanor. Danaus built his original temple and wooden statue; he also has the Amyclæan Apollo throne at Amyclæ, made by Bathycles.

sacrifice_to Aphrodite [burning the thighs of victims except wild boars] The Sicyonians preserved traditions about their rulers, foundations, tombs, temples, festivals, and sacred images. They became Dorians, joined the Achæan league under Aratus, and suffered a devastating earthquake that left the city nearly depopulated and destroyed many works of art.

l: Sicyonian royal succession, Description of Greece
s: Sicyonian royal succession runs from Epopeus through Lamedon and later rulers, ending when Phalces shares power with Lacestades after the Dorian seizure.

destroys Sicyon (city) [leaving it almost bare of men and destroying works of art] An earthquake struck Sicyon when the city's fortunes were already poor. It made the city almost bare of inhabitants and destroyed many works of art, while also damaging cities in Caria and Lycia and especially Rhodes.

l: Aratus's liberation of Sicyon, Description of Greece
s: Aratus entered Sicyon by night with refugees and Argive mercenaries, overcame the garrison and drove Nicocles out, then restored isonomy and property with compensation.

l: Cleomenes' war with the Achæans, Description of Greece
s: Cleomenes attacks and defeats the Achæans at Dyme, then violates agreements and expels Megalopolis’s inhabitants, compelling Aratus to seek Antigonus’s aid.

l: Battle of Sellasia, Description of Greece
s: is_won_by Antigonus [in concert with the Achæans] At Sellasia, Antigonus and the Achæans defeated Cleomenes after Cleomenes violated his terms with Antigonus. Sellasia was enslaved, Lacedæmon was captured, and the old political order of the Lacedæmonians was restored.

l: poisoning of Aratus, Description of Greece
s: is_committed_by Philip [unexpectedly] Philip secretly poisoned Aratus because Aratus criticized and sometimes restrained his violent behavior toward his subjects. Aratus died at Ægium, and his body was taken to Sicyon for burial in the hero-chapel called the Arateum.

contains_temple_of Athene Titane was reached by a narrow road from Sicyon and lay beyond the Asopus. It contained a mountain-top where the natives said Titan first dwelt, and it later became the site of Alexanor’s temple of Æsculapius.

Titan first dwelt on the mountain-top at Titane and gave it its name. Natives regarded him as the Sun’s brother because he was exceptionally skilled at observing seasons when the Sun fructified and ripened seeds and fruit.

Alexanor, son of Machaon and grandson of Æsculapius, comes to Sicyon, builds Æsculapius’s temple at Titane, perhaps makes its statue, and is later honored there with a statue and sunset sacrifices as a hero.
Machaon, son of Æsculapius, was killed by Eurypylus; Nestor recovered his bones, and he has a tomb, temple, sacred place, and bronze statue in Gerenia.

l: temple of Æsculapius at Titane, Description of Greece
s: At Titane, the temple of Æsculapius, built by Alexanor, son of Machaon and grandson of Æsculapius, stood in a precinct with old cypresses and mostly suppliant inhabitants. Its gables, porch, and interior contained figures of gods, heroes, and Æsculapius; partially concealed statues of Æsculapius and Hygiea, Alexanor, Euamerion, and Coronis also stood there. Sacred dragons lived within the precinct.

Pentathlum was an Olympic and athletic contest held at Olympia and other Greek games, including Delphi and Nemea; at Olympia it included a piper. It was remembered and added in the 18th Olympiad, when Lampis won. A boys’ pentathlum began in the 38th Olympiad but ended after Eutelidas of Lacedæmon won because Elis did not want boys training for it. Many athletes won it, including Gorgus, who won four Olympic victories, and Timon, who won at all Greek games except the Isthmian.

has_chief_town Phlius Phliasia lies next to Sicyonia, and its chief town is Phlius. The Phliasians are said to have been originally Argives and to have become Dorians after the return of the Heraclidæ.

The Phliasians are a people who say Aras first inhabited their land and founded Arantia. Originally Argives, they became Dorians after the Heraclidæ returned, preserve local traditions and Celeæ mysteries, honor Hebe, and are not connected with Arcadians.

The Arcadians are an indigenous people who inhabit Arcadia and have remained there continuously. Their central role is as persistent allies of the Messenians: they aided them in full force in the first Messenian War, rejected Spartan overtures, and supported them again in the second war, including at Boar’s Memorial and the Great Trench. At the Great Trench, however, their king Aristocrates, bribed by the Lacedæmonians, ordered a retreat; other Arcadians later exposed and stoned him. They welcomed surviving Messenians at Mount Lycæus, gave food, clothing, and offers of residence, helped restore Messene, and later fought beside them against the Lacedæmonians. After the capture of Megalopolis, fleeing Arcadians were received by the Messenians with equal rights. They also aided Elis in Hercules’s campaign, but later invaded Elis and were defeated after fleeing from a dragon-like portent.
Aras, an Autochthon and first inhabitant of Phliasian land, founded Arantia on the Arantine hill, named its land and city, fathered Aoris and Aræthyrea, and was buried at Celeæ.
is_a Dorian [son of Phalces] Rhegnidas, a Dorian and son of Phalces, marched against Phlius from Argos and Sicyon. He demanded kingship and the assignment of land to himself and the Dorians.
Hippasus leads Phliasians advocating vigorous resistance to Rhegnidas; when his people choose surrender, he flees with supporters to Samos.
is_descendant_of Hippasus [great-grandson] Pythagoras, surnamed the Wise, was the great-grandson of Hippasus. His ancestry is given as Hippasus, Euphron, Mnesarchus, and Pythagoras.
Celeæ, about five stades from Phlius, hosts the Phliasians’ fourth-year mysteries of Demeter and contains Aras’s and Dysaules’s tombs.

is_a town [small town on the road from Corinth to Argos] Cleonæ is a small town on the road from Corinth to Argos. It contains a temple of Athene with a statue attributed to Scyllis and Dipœnus, and a tomb of Eurytus and Cteatus.

Augeas, son of Eleus, rules Elis with shared administration and owns exceptionally numerous oxen and goats. Their dung blocks cultivation; after refusing Hercules' promised payment and expelling Phyleus, he faces defeat, forgiveness, and Phyleus' restoration.

Mycenæ, a place founded by Perseus after exchanging kingdoms with Megapenthes, was associated with a fallen scabbard or discovered fungus and water. Argives destroyed it from jealousy; its Thermopylæ contingent, ruins, lion gate, tombs, and underground treasuries remained.

Danaus wins Argos from Gelanor after the Argives read a wolf’s victory over a bull as an omen, with which he is identified. As king, he builds temples to Lycian Apollo and Athene, then tries his daughter Hypermnestra for sparing Lynceus.

is_killed_by Perseus [accidentally by a quoit throw at Larissa] Acrisius, son of Abas, retained Argos when he and his brother Prœtus divided the kingdom. He later went to Larissa, where Perseus unintentionally killed him with a quoit, fulfilling the prophecy that he had tried to avert.
Tiryns, in Prœtus’s kingdom, had visible palace remains and Cyclopean-built walls; it was destroyed by Argives after the Persian war.

is_a boxer [Rhodian; winner among men] Acusilaus, a son of Diagoras, won the Olympic boxing prize among men. He and his brother Damagetus came to Olympia with their father and carried him in celebration after their victories.

l: three Argive kingdoms, Description of Greece
s: are_ruled_by Anaxagoras [during his reign] The three Argive kingdoms arose during the reign of Anaxagoras after Melampus cured a madness affecting the women, in return for sharing the rule with his brother Bias. The native line descended from Anaxagoras, the line of Bias, and the line of Melampus supplied the three royal successions until Cylarabes became sole king.

Tisamenus is described both as Orestes and Hermione’s son, who succeeded Orestes and ruled Argos and Sparta until the Heraclidæ expelled him and his sons to Achaia, and as Thersander’s Iamide son, a prophet whose oracle-reading brought five wartime victories.
Son of Aristomachus, Cresphontes gains and rules Messenia after a disputed lot, establishes Stenyclerus, then wealthy opponents kill him and all but one son.

Aristodemus is presented as a king and member of the Æpytidæ, with records linking him both to Lacedæmon and to the Messenians. After offering and killing his daughter for a required sacrifice, he becomes king of the Messenians following Euphaes’s death. In the first Messenian War, he commands and deploys the Messenian forces from Ithome, seeks and interprets an omen from Delphi, then despairs of saving Messenia and kills himself at his daughter’s grave after six years and a few months. Another account says Pylades’ sons killed him.

l: claim of the Heraclidæ to Argos, Description of Greece
s: is_based_on descent from Perseus [as contrasted with Tisamenus’ descent from Pelops] The Heraclidæ claimed Argos on the ground that Tisamenus was descended from Pelops, whereas they descended from Perseus. They further argued that Hercules had killed Hippocoon and his sons and restored the country to Tyndareus, supporting their claim to the region.

Messenia is a country, named after Messene, wife of Polycaon, and said originally to have been uninhabited. It contains Ithome and has a border with Laconia, fixed by Augustus at Gerenia. Its early tradition includes sheltering Tyndareus, while the Heraclidæ claimed it because Hercules had entrusted it to Nestor and expelled Nestor’s descendants. Its central history is conflict with the Lacedæmonians: raids passed in both directions, then Ithome was evacuated and captured. Messenia was conquered, divided, and subjected to Spartan rule; its people surrendered half their produce, mourned Spartan kings and officials, and were largely expelled from the Peloponnese or reduced to servitude. After a general rising and nearly 300 years of exile, the Messenians were restored to Messenia.

Pylos is a mostly sandy place, associated with Neleus and called the city of Neleus. It was founded by Pylos, son of Cleson, who brought Leleges from Megaris, before Neleus and Pelasgians from Iolcus expelled him. Aphareus gave it to Neleus, who made it his seat of government; Nestor and his descendants later kept their royal court there. It has Athene Coryphasia’s temple, Nestor’s house and painting, Nestor’s tomb, and a cave said to be an ox-stall. Its men aided Elis and Pisa against Hercules, who later punished them.
Deiphontes, the son of Antimachus and a descendant of Hercules, served as Temenus's general and associate. He married Hyrnetho, whom Temenus favored above his other children.
A wolf, sent by Lycian Apollo, attacks cattle near Argos, defeats the leading bull, and becomes an omen of Danaus’s accession.

represents Gelanor [in the omen interpreted by the Argives] A bull leading a herd fought the wolf near the walls of Argos but was overcome. Its conflict with the wolf was represented in an amphitheatre near the temple of Lycian Apollo.

l: temple of Lycian Apollo, Description of Greece
s: The temple of Lycian Apollo, originally built by Danaus, contains his throne, statues and wooden images including Aphrodite and Hermes, the fire of Phoroneus, and other artworks; outside stand scenes of a wolf and bull and statues of Zeus and Artemis.

Hypermnestra, Danaus’s only daughter to spare her husband Lynceus, disobeys Danaus’s order to kill him. Danaus tries her, but the Argives acquit her. Afterward she dedicates a statue of Victorious Aphrodite; Artemis Persuasion is later associated with her victory in the trial. She signals safety from Larissa.

Telesilla is a poetess honored by the Argives for poetic gifts and defending Argos. After Cleomenes and the Lacedæmonians devastated Argos, she armed unfit slaves and women, led resistance, and compelled their withdrawal.

defeat Lacedæmonians [under Telesilla’s leadership] The Argive women were armed and led into battle by Telesilla after disaster had reduced Argos's defenders. They received the Lacedæmonian attack without dismay and forced the Lacedæmonians to yield.

is_a road The Hollow Way is a road in Argos. Along it are the temple of Dionysus, the house of Adrastus, the temple of Amphiaraus, the tomb of Eriphyle, and the shrine of Æsculapius; on the return route is the reputed tomb of Hyrnetho.

l: temple of Dionysus (on the Hollow Way), Description of Greece
s: A temple on the right side of the Hollow Way, dedicated to Dionysus, whose statue is said to have come from Eubœa.

l: cave of Dionysus, Description of Greece
s: The cave of Dionysus, refuge for wild goats from cold, was found by Argives surviving a shipwreck at Caphareus and contained a statue of Dionysus.

l: statue of Dionysus from the cave, Description of Greece
s: is_brought_to Argos [by the Argives after the winter] The Argives took the wooden statue of Dionysus from the cave after the winter ended and sailed home with it. They continued to worship it.
Bato, a Melampodid and relative of Amphiaraus, serves as his charioteer in battle and is swallowed by the earth with Amphiaraus and the chariot.

l: war between Dionysus and Perseus, Description of Greece
s: ends_in reconciliation [Dionysus and Perseus became friendly again] Dionysus was said to have warred with Perseus and later become friendly with him. Afterward, the Argives honored Dionysus in various ways and gave him the enclosure that became the temple of Cretan Dionysus.

l: temple of Cretan Dionysus, Description of Greece
s: Temple of Cretan Dionysus at Argos, dedicated after Dionysus was honoured by the Argives, was named for Ariadne’s burial; restoration reportedly revealed her ashes in an earthenware cinerary urn.

l: burial of Ariadne, Description of Greece
s: Ariadne’s burial was associated with the temple of Cretan Dionysus at Argos. An earthenware cinerary urn reportedly containing her ashes was found when the temple was restored.
Tegea, a place of repeated Lacedæmonian reverses, was later at peace when Lichas found Orestes’ bones; Pausanias received sanctuary at Alean Athene’s temple.
A division of the Peloponnese, always inhabited by Arcadians, Arcadia was later traversed by Dorians returning to the Peloponnese; its boundaries shifted from Pisa to Elis.

Ætolia was named after Ætolus, who fled there from the Peloponnese after unintentionally killing Apis. Oxylus later left Ætolia after accidentally killing his brother and introduced Ætolians as colonists into Elis.

l: Epidaurian sanctuary of Æsculapius, Description of Greece
s: The Epidaurian sanctuary of Æsculapius is a walled sacred district where no births or deaths occur, though sacrifices are consumed. Centered on Æsculapius’s temple and ivory-and-gold statue, it includes a sleeping-place for suppliants, healing inscriptions, Rotunda paintings, Polycletus’s theatre, Artemis and Maleatian Apollo temples, stadium, fountain, mountains, and Antonine additions. Its traditions culminate in healing, including Hippolytus’s restoration to life.

Ægina is an island, formerly called Œnone, said to be named for Ægina after Zeus brought her there; surrounding rocks and sunken reefs make access difficult, attributed to Æacus’s defense against pirates and enemies.
Thyrea is a place of battle contested by 300 Argives and 300 Lacedæmonians; the Lacedæmonians secured it, gave it to the Æginetans, and it was later inhabited and claimed as recovered by the Argives.

is_worshipped_at temple of Aphæa [on Ægina near Mount Pan-Hellenium] Aphæa is worshipped in Ægina, where she has a temple on the way to the mountain of Pan-Hellenian Zeus and where Pindar wrote an ode for the Æginetans. She is identified in the Cretan tradition with Britomartis, who is also called Dictynna in Crete.

Britomartis, daughter of Zeus and Carme, loved racing and hunting and befriended Artemis. Fleeing Minos, she fell into nets; Artemis made her a goddess, worshipped as Aphæa in Ægina and Dictynna in Crete.

Cerberus was described either as a deadly serpent reared at Tænarum or, by later writers, as a three-headed dog of Hades; tradition says Hercules brought the dog from the lower world through Tænarum's cave.

Hermione is a neighboring town in the Trœzenian region, with an old city on a rocky headland and a new city four stades away on a gentle slope. Its people say Hermion, son of Europs, founded it, and Dorians from Argos later colonized it amicably. It is especially marked by many temples, including those of Poseidon, Athene, Demeter, Proserpine, Apollo, Dionysus Melanægis, Artemis Iphigenia, and Demeter Chthonia, called most worthy of notice. It has two wells, uses Mases as its port, and its old well never runs dry.

has Methana warm baths [about 30 stades away] Methana was a small town on an isthmus jutting into the sea, with temples of Isis and statues of Hermes and Hercules. About thirty stades away were warm, very salty baths that appeared after fire bubbled from the ground during the reign of Antigonus, son of Demetrius. To protect their vines from the South West Wind, the people of Methana tore a white-feathered cock in half, carried the halves around the vines in opposite directions, and buried them where they met.

contains_temple_of Demeter Pron is the mountain on which Hermione’s temple of Demeter Chthonia stands. A road to Halice passes between Pron and Coccygium, and a temple of Hera stands on the top of Pron.

is_a Greek athletic games [held at Delphi and elsewhere in the account] The Pythian games are repeatedly compared with the Olympic games. Tisander had four boxing victories there, Milo had six victories among men and one among boys, Clitomachus won three pancratium victories, and several other athletes are recorded as winning in wrestling, boxing, the pentathlum, or running.
Chthonia, daughter of Colontas and sister of Clymenus, is brought to Hermione by Demeter, builds Demeter’s temple, and becomes Demeter’s epithet there.

The Chthonia is Hermione’s annual summer festival honouring Demeter Chthonia, unfolding through processions led by priests and town authorities with officials, women, men, and garlanded boys in white.

l: heifer sacrifice at Chthonia, Description of Greece
s: Heifer sacrifice is performed by priestesses of Demeter: a full-grown heifer is driven into the temple and killed with sickles, then three more are killed; completion requires all four fall on the first heifer’s side.
Mases, once a town mentioned by Homer among the Argives, serves as Hermione’s port in the narrator’s day.

Asine is a ruined seaside town in Messenia, formerly the chief town of Asinæa. Its Dryope inhabitants preserve their identity through annual mysteries of Dryops and a temple with an ancient statue. Descended from people defeated by Hercules, they settled first in Asine in Argolis, then in Messenia with Lacedæmonian permission. After aiding the Lacedæmonians against Argive territory, Asine was captured and razed by the Argives, though Apollo’s temple remained.
Amymone, Danaus’s daughter, lends her name to a river that bounds a sacred grove at Lerna and rises near a plane-tree.

The hydra, a monster said to be reared beneath a plane-tree near the Amymone’s source, infested the river; it was larger than ordinary water-snakes, venomous, and described by Pisander as many-headed.
Alcyonian marsh near Lerna is an unfathomably deep, dangerous marsh, believed by the Argives to be Dionysus’s descent to Hades to bring up Semele; its secret annual nightly rites remain undescribed.

Temenium is a fortified place belonging to the Argives, named for Temenus, who occupied and fortified it fighting with the Dorians against Tisamenus and the Achæans; Phrixus reaches the sea there, beside temples and Temenus’s monument.

The Achæans, an indigenous Peloponnese group, were driven from their original land by the Dorians, displaced Ionians in Ægialus, later called Achaia, and some colonized Elis with Agorius. Openly hostile to the Lacedæmonians, they fought with and later attacked the Messenians, but Dinocrates forced their withdrawal. At Olympia they dedicated statues of heroes who drew lots to face Hector, claiming descent from Pelops.
Polycaon, younger son of Lelex, married Messene, ruled the land later called Messenia from Andania, and was later criticized with her for neglecting Zeus on Ithome.

Amyclæ is a village reached by the road from Sparta, past the Tiasa and a temple of the Graces. Destroyed by the Dorians, it remains notable for the sanctuary of Amyclæan Apollo, rites for Apollo at the festival of Hyacinthus, and weaving Apollo’s coat. Its chief gods are Apollo and Dionysus Psilax. Its monuments include Ænetus’s statue, tripods from Ægos-potamoi, statues and a temple of Alexandra, representations of Clytæmnestra and Agamemnon, and Agamemnon’s supposed tomb.

Hyacinthus is a very handsome, small-bearded figure with a virgin sister, Polybœa. He is buried beneath Apollo’s statue at Amyclæ, where offerings precede sacrifices to Apollo during Hyacinthia. An altar shows gods carrying him and Polybœa to heaven; traditions report his accidental death by Apollo but may be baseless.

rules Messenia [with Leucippus; Aphareus had greater power] Aphareus succeeded Perieres as king with his brother Leucippus and held the greater power. He built Arene, received Neleus, and learned the mysteries of the Great Goddesses from Lycus.
Thalamæ is a place about eighty stades by road from Œtylus, centered on a temple and dream oracle of Ino, with bronze statues, including Pasiphae and the Sun, and the Moon’s sacred spring.
Eurysthenes, elder twin son of Aristodemus, became ancestor of the Agidæ and jointly helped Theras establish a colony on Thera.

Agesilaus, son of Doryssus, was a Lacedæmonian king during Lycurgus’ legislation. He returned to Corinth with an army, lost Amyclæan troops to Athenians, compelled Acarnanians to end war after marching into Ætolia, aided revolted Egyptians, and died sailing home; the Lacedæmonians honoured his burial.
Teleclus was a Lacedæmonian king and hero-chapel occupant; accounts differ whether he died protecting maidens at Artemis Limnas or plotting against Messenians with disguised armed youths.
Theopompus, son of Nicander and king of the Lacedæmonians, succeeded Nicander, befriended the Phocians, and led the right wing against the Messenians, suffering defeat before fighting Euphaes again.

Lichas, a Lacedæmonian son of Arcesilaus, entered and won an Olympic chariot-race as a Theban during Lacedæmonian exclusion, was scourged for binding the charioteer, prompted an invasion of Elis, and later erected a statue at Olympia.

Dorieus, son of Anaxandrides and half-brother of Cleomenes, Leonidas, and Cleombrotus, was judged superior in counsel and war but denied kingship; refusing subjection to Cleomenes, he led a colonizing expedition to Sicily.

Demaratus was a well-regarded Spartan king who cooperated with Cleomenes in freeing Athens from the Pisistratidæ. Cleomenes’ hatred, Aristo’s statement about his birth, and a bribed priestess led to his unjust deposition. He then went to Persia to serve Darius.
Leotychides became king after Demaratus, fought at Mycale and in Thessaly, accepted payment from the Aleuadæ, was impeached, exiled himself to Tegea, and was succeeded by Archidamus.

Aristo, son of Agesicles, said that his newborn son Demaratus could not be his because the child was born seven months after the marriage. He later regretted the statement, but it was used against Demaratus in the dispute that deprived him of the kingship.

is_a Lacedæmonian force [at Thermopylæ] Leonidas’ 300 Lacedæmonians met Xerxes’ army at Thermopylæ. They were overcome only after a Trachinian showed the barbarians a route around Mount Œta to the Greek flank.

commands Athenians [against Pausanias at Thebes] Thrasybulus was associated with the Athenians opposing the later Pausanias. Pausanias withdrew from Attica partly because he feared being caught between the Athenians and forces led by Thrasybulus.

Lysander, a Spartan and son of Aristocritus, was a military leader whose victories over Antiochus near Ephesus and over the Athenian navy at Aegospotami brought him honor. The Samians erected and inscribed a praising statue for him at Olympia, while Ephesians set up statues after Aegospotami; he also dedicated eagles and victories. He especially opposed Leonidas and helped bring about his deposition. Marching into Phocis and attacking Haliartus, he was killed by Thebans and Athenians.

The Messenians are a people of Messenia whose history is marked by repeated war, defeat, exile, return, and continuing resistance to the Lacedæmonians. They revolted during Anaxander’s reign and killed Teleclus in the temple of Artemis Limnas. After Amphea fell, they gathered at Stenyclerus under Euphaes, fought with Arcadian help, suffered losses and pestilence, and withdrew to Ithome. Although they defeated the Lacedæmonians with their allies, Aristodemus’s death preceded the evacuation of Ithome. They were compelled to pay Sparta half their land’s produce and observe mourning requirements. They later rose again under Aristomenes. Early successes ended in disaster at the Great Trench when Aristocrates withdrew the Arcadians. The Messenians retreated to Eira, raided Laconia and Messenia, and resisted siege for eleven years; Aristomenes hid sacred records on Mount Ithome in hope of recovery. Eira’s final three-day defense involved even the women, amid hunger, thirst, cold, rain, and exhaustion. Its capture led to some Messenians becoming Helots, while others escaped to Arcadia and later founded a settlement in Sicily. After a second defeat they evacuated the Peloponnese; many remaining there became slaves. In another revolt they held Ithome, received Naupactus from the Athenians, conquered Œniadæ, broke through its Acarnanian blockade, and used Naupactus against the Peloponnese, including by assisting the Athenians at Sphacteria. Most exiles later settled in Euesperitæ. After nearly 300 years, or 287 years after Eira’s capture, they returned, rebuilt their country, retained their customs and Doric dialect, and again resisted Sparta. They received Macedonian aid under Philip, captured and controlled Elis after expelling its Lacedæmonian party, and eventually joined the Achæan League. They sheltered Arcadians after Megalopolis, joined Aratus at Sellasia, captured Philopœmen, punished those responsible for his death, and rejoined the League. Their Victory monument at Olympia commemorated their share at Sphacteria but omitted the enemy’s name from fear. Olympic success declined in exile and resumed after restoration, with Damiscus’s victory.

l: Dorians' return to the Peloponnese, Description of Greece
s: During the Dorians’ planned return to the Peloponnese, an oracle instructed them to choose a three-eyed man as leader. They accepted Oxylus, followed his advice to travel by ship, and agreed to give him the kingdom of Elis.

l: first Messenian War, Description of Greece
s: The first Messenian War was a twenty-year conflict between the Messenians and Lacedæmonians. It began with a Lacedæmonian night attack and capture of Amphea during Euphaes’ reign, with Theopompus playing a leading role on the Lacedæmonian side. At its height under Polydorus, it involved repeated battles, raids, sieges, bribery, omens, divine assistance, and resistance associated with Aristomenes, including defeat at the Great Trench and resistance at Eira. It ended with Ithome’s capture and evacuation, followed by Lacedæmonian conquest, tribute, submission oaths, and compulsory mourning.

The Messenian revolt occurred during the reign of Anaxander, son of Eurycrates. The Messenians fought the Lacedæmonians for some time but were eventually conquered and expelled from the Peloponnese under conditions of war.

l: Battle of Platæa, Description of Greece
s: At Platæa, Pausanias led the Lacedæmonians as Greeks fought Mardonius, Medes, and barbarians. After Mardonius fell, the barbarians were annihilated; Pausanias protected his body and returned a Coan woman to Cos. Greeks later commemorated victory at Olympia with a Zeus statue.

is_attributed_to Lycurgus [for the Lacedæmonians] Lycurgan legislation was enacted during the reign of Agesilaus by Lycurgus. The text preserves competing accounts that Lycurgus learned the laws from Crete or received instruction from the oracle at Delphi.

Spartan kingship was a divided monarchy in Lacedæmon, held by two royal houses descended from Procles and Eurysthenes, twin sons of Aristodemus. Though succession generally favored primogeniture, it repeatedly faced disputes and depositions, ending with Cleomenes, son of Leonidas.

is_shared_by Messenia [temple on the border of Messenia and Laconia] The temple of Artemis Limnas stood on the border of Messenia and was shared by the Messenians and Lacedæmonians as the only Dorians with a share there. Conflicting traditions about an incident at the temple involving maidens, Teleclus, and Messenians became part of the causes alleged for the later war.

l: Cleomenes (son of Leonidas), Description of Greece
s: was_last_king_of Agiadæ [at Sparta] Cleomenes, son of Leonidas, was the last Agiad king at Sparta. His deeds, bravery, and the end of the Spartan kings are said to have been recorded previously in connection with Aratus of Sicyon, including the details of his death in Egypt.

Archidamus is a Spartan king described in conflicting accounts as either grandson of Leotychides or son of Agesilaus. One reign features invasions of Attica, the capture of Platæa, and succession by Agis; another centers on aiding the Phocians after their seizure of Delphi’s temple while preventing Delphi’s destruction. He dies fighting barbarians near Tarentum.

Agesilaus, son of Archidamus and a Spartan king, was chosen over Leotychides despite an oracle. He commanded land forces in Asia Minor, defeated Tissaphernes near the Hermus, became fleet commander, returned during the Corinthian War, defeated Thebans and allies at Coronea, and honored Athene Itonia while wounded.

l: Lysander (son of Aristocritus), Description of Greece
s: violated Peloponnesian War [by violating the oaths with the Athenians] Lysander, son of Aristocritus, helped persuade the Lacedæmonians to choose Agesilaus as king. He and Agis violated their oaths with the Athenians after the destruction of the Athenian fleet and agreed with their allies to destroy Athens; his death occurred during the events later associated with the Corinthian War.
Cyrus supplied the Lacedæmonians with money for their ships during the war against the Athenians. The Lacedæmonians learned that Cyrus, rather than Artaxerxes, had provided this support.

Persia was the target of the Lacedæmonian expedition led by Agesilaus. Its king Artaxerxes responded to Agesilaus’ advance by redirecting leadership in Asia Minor and financing opposition to Sparta in Greece.

Tissaphernes was satrap of Ionia and commanded the Persian army against Agesilaus near the Hermus. Agesilaus defeated his cavalry and infantry, after which Artaxerxes condemned Tissaphernes to death and gave his satrapy to Tithraustes.

Sardis was the principal city of wealthy Lydia and the chief residence of the satrap by the sea. Agesilaus marched there after crossing to Asia Minor and later defeated Tissaphernes in the plain near the Hermus.
The Corinthian War began with the Lacedæmonian invasion of Bœotia, compelled Agesilaus to return from Asia Minor, and ended with his victory over the Thebans and allies at Coronea.

The Olympian games are a festival of athletic and horse-racing contests at Olympia, associated with ancient traditions of their institution or renewal by figures including Idæan Hercules and Iphitus. According to the archives of Elis, Idæan Hercules set them every fifth year after racing his four brothers; other traditions connect them with Zeus, Cronos, and other early founders. The games had been discontinued after the reign of Oxylus, then Iphitus restored them with the people of Elis after instructions from the priestess at Delphi. After revival, their programme expanded from running to the double course, pentathlum, wrestling, boxing, horse-races, pancratium, boys' contests, the race in heavy armour, and races for colts. Some events were later ended, including the pentathlum for boys and, in the 84th Olympiad, the chariot and trotting races. The contests reward merit, speed, and bodily strength rather than money. Bribery, accepting bribes, lateness, and cowardice brought punishments and fines, often used for statues of Zeus. Victors receive wild-olive crowns, prizes, memorial statues or chariots, and a banquet in the Town Hall of the people of Elis. The priestess of Demeter Chamyne watches from a white-stone altar opposite the umpires, while arrangements for horse-racing starts aim at fairness. The games also preserve many individual victories and disputes over victory lists. Control of the games is contested. Pisa sought to conduct them instead of Elis in the eighth and thirty-fourth Olympiads, and Arcadians held games in the 104th; Elis excluded these games from its registers. Thus the games unfold as a repeatedly renewed festival: restored after suspension, enlarged through new contests, governed through rules and penalties, celebrated through victors and crowns, and defended by Elis against rival oversight.

l: invasion of Asia, Description of Greece
s: The Lacedæmonians resolved to invade Asia and attack Artaxerxes, sending Agesilaus as commander of the land forces. The expedition reached Asia Minor and achieved victories, but the Corinthian War forced Agesilaus to bring the army back to Greece.

l: Battle of Coronea, Description of Greece
s: was_won_by Agesilaus [against the Thebans and their allies] At Coronea, Agesilaus and the Lacedæmonians defeated the Thebans and their allies after returning from Asia. Agesilaus was wounded, but he did not violate the sanctuary of Athene Itonia when some defeated Bœotians fled there.

l: market-place of Sparta, Description of Greece
s: contains Spartan Senate [a council chamber for the Senate] The market-place of Sparta contained the council chamber, public buildings for the Ephors, guardians of the laws, and Bidiæi, and the notable Persian Portico built from spoils taken from the Medes. It also held statues of Persian figures, Artemisia, Pythæan Apollo, Artemis, Leto, Agias, and the People of Sparta, along with temples of several gods and monuments connected with Orestes, Polydorus, and other figures. The text further describes the Scias and several roads and shrines leading from the market-place.
Perieres, son of Æolus, became king of Messenia after Polycaon’s descendants died out, received Melaneus, and fathered Aphareus and Leucippus with Gorgophone.

Alpheus is a large, pleasant river rising in Arcadia, not Elis. It has seven notable tributaries, including Helisson, Brentheates, Gortynius, Buphagus, Ladon, Erymanthus, and Cladeus, and later receives Diagon and Lucyanias as it flows through Pylos in Elis. It matters especially at Olympia: seers use it to renew the great altar, it is considered particularly friendly to Olympian Zeus, and it has altars with Artemis and alone. Traditions describe it as a hunter loving Arethusa, flowing under the sea to Ortygia, and unsuccessfully pursuing Artemis at Letrini.

l: battle of Ægos-potamoi, Description of Greece
s: The battle of Ægos-potamoi was an Athenian fleet defeat and capture, after which Samians dedicated a statue of Lysander and Ephesians honored Spartans; later Conon’s victories prompted Ionians to shift allegiance and honor Conon and Timotheus.

l: Phocian seizure of Delphi, Description of Greece
s: The Phocian seizure of Delphi occurred during the reign of Archidamus. It prompted competing offers of aid to the Thebans and public support for the Phocians from the Lacedæmonians and Athenians. The Phocians planned extreme violence against the inhabitants of Delphi, but Archidamus prevented the massacre, enslavement, and destruction.

Tænarum is a promontory with the harbours Achilleus and Psamathus, a cave-like temple of Poseidon, and a bronze Arion riding a dolphin. Its fountain once revealed harbours and ships, but lost this power after dirty linen was washed in it; Cænepolis was formerly called Tænarum.

is_a running practice of the young men [the place where young men still practise running] The Lacedæmonians call Dromus the place where young men still practise running. It contains gymnasiums and is near monuments and temples including the sepulchre of Eumedes, a statue of Hercules, and temples of Castor and Pollux, the Graces, Ilithyia, Carnean Apollo, and Sovereign Artemis.

Spartan youths are a group that practise running at Dromus and fight at Platanistas. Before fighting, each division sacrifices a puppy dog to Enyalius and pits tame boars; the victorious boar’s party is generally victorious. Next day, lot-assigned approaches cross bridges, followed by hand-and-foot combat involving biting, eye-tearing, and pushing into water.

l: Castor and Pollux, Description of Greece
s: oppose Messenians [before the battle at Stenyclerus; later appeased] Castor and Pollux were believed to have become hostile to the Messenians after Panormus and Gonippus profaned their festival by disguising themselves as the Twin Brethren and killing Lacedæmonians. Their wrath was later said to have been appeased, and the Messenians sacrificed to them during the restoration.

is_a fights of the youths [a place surrounded by water like an island and enclosed by continuous plane-trees] Platanistas is a place surrounded by water like an island and enclosed by continuous plane-trees. The young men enter it by bridges and fight there with hands and feet, biting, tearing out one another’s eyes, violently attacking one another, and pushing opponents into the water.

l: fights of the youths, Description of Greece
s: The fights of the youths take place at Platanistas after sacrifices to Enyalius at the temple of Phœbus. The divisions approach by routes assigned by lot on the previous night, and the youths fight with hands and feet, bite and tear at one another, and push one another into the water.

contains the temple of Menelaus Therapne is named after Therapne, the daughter of Lelex, and contains a temple of Menelaus where the Lacedæmonians say Menelaus and Helen were buried. It also has the fountain Messeis, while the fountain Polydeucea and the temple of Polydeuces lie on the road to it. Nearby are temples of Phœbus, Poseidon, and other divinities.

Iphitus, a relative of Oxylus and contemporary of Lycurgus, revived and renewed the Olympian games with Elis after their suspension. Directed by Delphi, he established their truce, persuaded Elis to sacrifice to Hercules, and served as sole original umpire. He is depicted crowned by Ecechiria and possessed an inscribed quoit.

l: Athene Poliuchus and Chalciœcus, Description of Greece
s: Athene Poliuchus and Chalciœcus is a deity whose temple stood on Sparta’s citadel. Tradition says Tyndareus began it and the Lacedæmonians completed it. Gitiadas made her bronze statue and decorated the temple; Aristomenes hung a shield there. The surrounding citadel held other temples, statues, and figures.

is_in Italy Rhegium was ruled by Anaxilas, who invited the Messenian exiles there before conveying them to Sicily. Anaxilas used the conflict between Rhegium and Zancle as the basis for the Messenians’ settlement.

Bathycles of Magnesia was an artist who, aided by Magnesians, made Amyclæan Apollo’s throne, carving Graces and Artemis Leucophryene amid extensive scenes of gods, heroes, myths, contests, battles, animals, and exploits.
The Messenian war, involving Lacedæmonians with allies and Messenians with mercenaries, is named for Messenian disasters and runs from Amphea’s capture to Aristodemus’s death and beyond.

l: Orthian Artemis cult, Description of Greece
s: uses_human_blood human sacrifice at Artemis's altar [later replaced by flogging] The Orthian Artemis cult at Limnæum centered on a wooden image believed by the Lacedæmonians to be the statue stolen from the Tauric Chersonese by Orestes and Iphigenia. The cult was linked to an old tradition of human sacrifice: after conflicts and killings at the altar, an oracle required human blood, but Lycurgus replaced the sacrifice with the flogging of young men. During the flogging, the priestess held the statue, which was said to become heavy whenever the scourgers spared a young man because of beauty or rank; the goddess was also called Bound-with-willow-twigs because willows had held the image upright.

l: Amyclæan Apollo throne, Description of Greece
s: The throne of Amyclæan Apollo is an object covered with mythological carvings. Graces and Seasons stand at its front and back, while Hydra and Typhos occupy the left and Tritons the right. Its scenes include Atlas; Hercules’ contests, labors, and victory over the Nemean lion; Perseus and Medusa; Theseus leading the Minotaur; gods bringing gifts to Harmony; Achilles fighting Memnon; Bellerophon killing the Chimæra; and other figures and episodes. Beneath the throne, carvings continue with the Calydonian boar, Calais and Zetes driving away the Harpies, Helen’s abduction, Apollo and Artemis killing Tityus, and Trojan offerings at Hector’s grave.

l: Lacedæmonian temples and hero-chapels, Description of Greece
s: The Lacedæmonians maintained many temples and hero-chapels, including those of Cynisca, Alcimus, Enaræphorus, Dorceus, Sebrus, Alcman, Helen, Hercules, Œonus, Athene, Hipposthenes, Cadmus and his descendants, Amphilochus, Poseidon, Cleodæus, Œbalus, Æsculapius, Teleclus, Aphrodite, Hilaira and Phœbe, Chilo, Lycurgus, Orthian Artemis, Ilithyia, Ammon, the Graces, and others. They erected statues and monuments to commemorate victories, heroes, laws, myths, and divine protection, and they followed oracles in establishing or altering several of these rites and dedications.

The Eleutherolacones were a group inhabiting maritime Laconia, holding 18 cities. Emperor Augustus liberated them from rule imposed by the Lacedæmonians of Sparta. Their towns included Zarax and Brasiæ; Las joined their council despite Messenian inhabitants, and Zarax was ravaged after Cleonymus destroyed it.

l: the temple of Apollo at Amyclæ, Description of Greece
s: The temple of Apollo at Amyclæ contains a throne with several partitions and intervals, the largest of which is in the middle and supports Apollo’s statue. The base of the statue is like an altar and is said to contain the burial of Hyacinthus; the altar is decorated with figures of numerous gods and mythological figures, including Hyacinthus and Polybœa being carried to heaven.

l: the statue of Apollo at Amyclæ, Description of Greece
s: The statue of Apollo at Amyclæ is an ancient, inartistic work, not made by Bathycles, conjectured to be about 30 cubits high. Like a brazen pillar except for face, toes, and hands, it wears a helmet, holds lance and bow, and stands on Hyacinthus’s tomb-like altar base.
Malea is a promontory that sailors round after leaving Bœæ. A tradition at Pyrrhichus says that Silenus came from Malea, and Pindar is quoted as calling Silenus Malea-born.
Epidelium is a place on the borders of Bœæ, beyond Malea, containing Apollo’s temple and a wooden Apollo statue cast into the sea during Delos’s sack.
Menophanes, a general of Mithridates, destroys Delos, killing inhabitants and robbing merchants and temples; escaped merchants then ambush him, sink his vessel, and kill him.

Epidaurus Limera, adjacent to Bœæ and about two hundred stades from Epidelium, was said to be founded by Epidaurians from Argolis rather than Lacedæmonians. Its notable sights unfold through temples, an Æsculapius altar and stone statue, the water of Ino, harbour-side Zeus Soter, citadel Athene, and sea-jutting Minoa.

Zarax, about one hundred stades from Epidaurus Limera, has a convenient harbour. Cleonymus especially ravaged it among Eleutherolacones towns; its chief remaining sight is a harbour-end temple of Apollo with a lyre-holding statue.

Brasiæ, formerly Oreatæ, was the last Eleutherolaconian place on that coast, about two hundred stades from Cyphanta. Its people said Semele and Dionysus arrived in a chest; Dionysus was reared in Ino’s cave, inspiring its renamed identity, garden, and temples to Æsculapius and Achilles.

Las is a town ten stades from the sea and forty from Gythium, between Ilium, Asia, and Cnacadium. Its sights include temples of Athene, Carnean Apollo, Dionysus, and Æsculapius, Galaco’s milky water, and the tomb and statue of its founder Las, killed by Patroclus.

Pyrrhichus is a town in the heart of the country, about forty stades inland from the river Scyras. Said to be named for Pyrrhus or the god of the Curetes, it preserves traditions of Silenus and temples of Artemis and Apollo Amazonius.

Pephnos is a seaside place about twenty stades from Thalamæ, with a small same-named island. Thalamæ’s people say Castor and Pollux were born there; small open-air bronze statues of them withstand winter waves unmoved.

Cardamyle is a city Homer named among Agamemnon’s promised gifts; detached from Messenia by Augustus, it became subject to Sparta and has a Nereus-daughters grove and temples of Athene and Carnean Apollo.

Gerenia, formerly called Enope by Homer and Chœrian dell in the author's time, is a Messenian city whose people join the Eleutherolacones' council. Traditions place Nestor's upbringing or flight there after Hercules took Pylos; it holds Machaon's tomb, temple, and bronze statue.

Messene, daughter of Triopas and wife of Polycaon, helped invade and name Messenia, lived at Andania, and was said to establish games for the Great Goddesses. Later, during restoration of the Messenian capital, priests and leaders invoked her to return and dwell with the Messenians.

hosts mysteries of the Great Goddesses [in ancient times and in the author's time] Andania was the royal headquarters of Polycaon and Messene and was the place where the mysteries of the Great Goddesses were celebrated in ancient times. Lycus introduced the mysteries there to Aphareus, his sons, and Arene.
The Great Goddesses' mysteries came from Eleusis to Messenia through Caucon, were taught by Lycus, honoured more highly, and continued as annual rites at Andania.
Arene, built by Aphareus and named for Œbalus’s daughter, housed Aphareus and his sons before Lycus arrived fleeing Athens.

is_a town [in Messenia, about 80 stades from Abia] Pharæ lay about 80 stades from Abia and about six stades from the sea. Its traditions included Pharis as founder, the healing powers of Nicomachus and Gorgasus, a temple and statue of Fortune, and the first known statue of Fortune by Bupalus.
Æpytus, youngest son and sole surviving heir of Cresphontes, is raised by Cypselus, restored to Messenia, punishes his family’s murderers, gains support, and founds the Æpytidæ line.

is_royal_residence_of Cresphontes [chosen by Cresphontes] Stenyclerus became the royal residence under Cresphontes, replacing the earlier centers at Andania, Arene, and Pylos. Cresphontes built his palace there for himself and his sons.

Mothone, formerly called Pedasus, was inhabited by Nauplia after the Nauplians’ expulsion. Its inhabitants linked its later name to Mothone, daughter of Œneus, but the account favors the Rock of Mothon, whose narrowing entrance makes a harbour and breakwater. Trajan granted it a free constitution; it has temples and a pitch-mixed well.

is_king_of Messenia [jointly with Antiochus before their civil conflict] Androcles, son of Phintas and fellow king of Messenia, argued that Polychares should be surrendered because of his violent conduct. His dispute with Antiochus led to armed conflict between their supporters, and Antiochus’ party killed him and his leading partisans.
Polychares, a Messenian Olympic victor and cattle-owner, entrusts cattle to Euæphnus; after their sale and his son's killing, denied justice in Lacedæmon, he attacks Lacedæmonians.

is_spartan Sparta [cattle-keeper for Polychares] Euæphnus was a Spartan entrusted by Polychares with cattle but sold them to merchants and falsely claimed that pirates had taken them. After being exposed, he lured and killed Polychares’ son, becoming the central figure in the dispute over whether Polychares should be surrendered.
